title: FRM Operational, Lesson 5: External loss data - borrowing someone else's tail
subtitle: Why you cannot take another bank's figure straight off the page, and how to scale it properly
whyItMatters: External data is the only source containing events large enough to shape the tail. But it comes from firms of a different size, a different business mix and a different control quality - and how that difference is handled drives the final capital number more than any modelling choice does.
openingQuestion: A small bank sees a 5,000bn loss event in the industry data, at a bank ten times its size. How should that figure enter their model?
openingOptions: Enter the full 5,000bn, because that event could perfectly well happen to them
Scale it for size and business mix before it goes in
Ignore it, since the event happened at another firm and has no bearing on them
Spread it over ten years to smooth its effect on the distribution
explanation: A payment fraud event at a bank with ten times the transaction volume produces a very different loss figure than the same kind of event at a smaller bank - simply because a different amount of money moves through the system. But ignoring it entirely is wrong too, since that is a class of event that can strike anyone. The standard treatment is to scale by an appropriate size variable, usually revenue or transaction volume, while separately assessing whether your own control environment is comparable.

realWorldExample.description: Databases run by an industry consortium collect losses from many member firms and return the data anonymised. They are more complete than press-derived sources but still carry a minimum collection threshold, so everything below it is truncated - and unless that truncation is handled when the distribution is fitted, the model will estimate frequency lower than it really is.

quiz.question: Why is loss data from public sources biased relative to reality?
options: Because only losses large enough or scandalous enough get published
Because firms always publish a figure higher than the true one
Because publication always lags the event by several years
Because public sources only record credit risk losses
quiz.explanation: This is reporting bias: small events are handled internally and never leave the building. Fitting a distribution to public data without accounting for that cut-off produces something that looks fatter-tailed than reality in severity, and thinner than reality in frequency. Firms have no incentive to overstate, credit losses are a separate category with their own disclosure rules, and reporting delay shifts the timing of an observation rather than which observations exist.

quiz.question: Scenario: a 5,000bn event at a bank with ten times the revenue. What does linear scaling by revenue give?
options: 5,000bn (= unchanged, since risk does not depend on size)
500bn (= 5,000 ÷ 10, scaled by the size ratio)
50,000bn (= 5,000 × 10, multiplying instead of dividing)
1,000bn (= 5,000 ÷ 5, using the wrong scaling factor)
quiz.explanation: Linear scaling divides in proportion to the size variable: 5,000 ÷ 10 = 500bn. In practice the relationship is usually sub-linear - a firm ten times larger does not suffer losses ten times larger - so an exponent below 1 is commonly used, and the choice of that exponent moves the result a great deal.

quiz.question: Besides size, what else has to be adjusted for when borrowing external data?
options: The headcount of the risk management function on either side
The exchange rate at the moment the event was disclosed publicly
The quality of your own firm's control environment relative to theirs
The credit rating of the firm that disclosed the loss event
quiz.explanation: Two firms of the same size, one with tight segregation of duties and one without, have quite different probabilities of the event occurring. Leaving this dimension out means implicitly assuming every firm of a given size carries the same risk - and once you assume that, money spent on controls can never show up in the capital number. Headcount, exchange rates and credit ratings say nothing about whether the control actually works.

quiz.question: Why does the minimum collection threshold of an industry database cause a problem when fitting a distribution?
options: Because member firms report in a number of different currencies
Because the small events make up most of the total loss value
Because the threshold changes each year, so nothing is comparable
Because the data is truncated below the collection threshold
quiz.explanation: Below the threshold the data is not zero, it is unobserved - two entirely different things. Fitting as though this were the whole sample misestimates both the frequency and the shape of the distribution; the correct treatment is to fit a distribution conditional on exceeding the threshold and then infer the part below. Currency conversion is a mechanical fix, small events are by definition not most of the value, and thresholds are generally stable.

quiz.question: What is the main role of external data in an operational risk model?
options: Supplying the tail that internal data does not contain
Replacing internal data entirely, because the sample is far larger
Confirming the frequency figures computed internally
Meeting the periodic reporting requirement set by the regulator
quiz.explanation: Internal data describes the body of the distribution better than any other source, because it is literally your own firm. What it does not have is the tail, and that is exactly the gap industry data fills - using it in place of the body would throw away everything specific to your own organisation. It is not a validation exercise for internal frequency estimates, and no regulator asks for it as a reporting artefact.

practicePrompt.question: You borrow a 5,000bn loss event from a bank with ten times your revenue. Linear scaling gives 500bn. Why is that figure usually too low?
options: Because losses scale sub-linearly with the size of the firm
Because large banks always have distinctly better controls
Because public data only records the direct portion of the damage
Because exchange rates and inflation between the two dates are unadjusted
practicePrompt.explanation: The relationship between size and operational loss is sub-linear: a firm ten times larger does not suffer losses ten times larger, because most large events attach to a particular process or a particular person rather than expanding with revenue. An unauthorised trading incident or a botched deployment does roughly the same damage in either place. Dividing straight by 10 therefore cuts too deep. The exponent commonly used sits somewhere around 0.5 to 0.8, and it has to be paired with a second adjustment for the difference in control quality - otherwise money spent on controls never shows up in the capital.

keyTakeaways: External data fills in the tail that internal data lacks; it does not replace the body
It has to be scaled by a size variable, and usually sub-linearly rather than linearly
It also has to be adjusted for the difference in control quality, or investment in controls never shows up in capital
Collection thresholds truncate the data from below - fit conditionally, not as a complete sample

summary.keyIdea: Borrowing someone else's data is the only way to see the tail, but every borrowed figure has to pass two questions: is the size comparable, and is the control environment comparable.

application.message: When you see an operational risk model using industry data, ask what the size scaling exponent is and why that number was chosen. It is a parameter with a heavy influence on the result and it is rarely explained.

sections.text: No firm has enough catastrophes of its own to build a tail from. So people borrow from each other - and the whole difficulty is that the borrowed figure is not your figure.
Two kinds of source, two kinds of bias

Public sources draw on the press and on court filings: only events large enough or loud enough get in, so the data is artificially fat-tailed. Consortium databases are more complete because members report events that were never made public, but they still have a minimum threshold, so everything below it disappears - and disappearing is not the same as being zero.
Scaling for size, and why it is not linear

Intuition says a firm ten times larger suffers losses ten times larger. In practice it is usually less than that: a large firm has more layers of control, detects problems earlier, and many kinds of loss have a natural ceiling that does not stretch with size. So an exponent below 1 is commonly used - and that choice moves the result more than most of the technical choices around it.

Two banks of the same size but differing in segregation of duties, in limits, and in supervisory quality have very different event probabilities. If the model adjusts for size alone, it is implicitly saying controls make no difference - and once it says that, no amount spent on controls can ever reduce a single unit of capital.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: Data below the collection threshold is not zero, it is unobserved. Fitting a distribution as though this were a complete sample gets both the frequency and the shape wrong.
